memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: The men turned away and went toward Sodom, but Abraham remained standing before the Lord. Then Abraham approached him and said: "Will you sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" - Gen 18:22-23 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
The visitors turn toward Sodom, but Abraham "remained standing before the Lord." He does not go about his business, relieved that judgement is falling on someone else's city. Instead, he lingers in God's presence and dares to intercede - pleading for a wicked city where his nephew Lot lives. Abraham becomes a man standing in the gap.

This is one of the most remarkable pictures of intercessory prayer in all of Scripture. Abraham had every reason to let Sodom face its fate. It was a wicked place; its people had wronged and endangered his family. Yet his heart is moved to plead for mercy, even for the undeserving.

Notice how the prayer begins: with a concern for justice - "Will you sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" Abraham's intercession is not selfish. He is gripped by God's own character, appealing to God on the basis of who God is.

Here we see a foreshadowing of something greater. Abraham stood in the gap for a doomed city; Jesus stands in the gap for a doomed world, "always liv[ing] to intercede" for us (Heb 7:25). And we are called to this ministry too - to linger before God and plead for others, even the undeserving, even those the world would write off. Who is God calling you to stand in the gap for today?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
- Do you linger before God to intercede for others, or move on to your own concerns?
- Who might God be calling you to "stand in the gap" for?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Lord, thank You that Jesus ever lives to intercede for me. Give me a heart like Abraham's, willing to stand in the gap and plead for others, even the undeserving. Show me who to pray for today.
Amen.
